raw_case_text:
A 10-year-old male child presented to our surgery clinic on October 2021 with a chief complaint of abdominal pain and vomiting for the past ten months. The pain was frequent, colicky, postprandial, and generalized. It was aggravated by eating and associated with vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss. There was no history of hematuria, rectal bleeding, or diarrhea. There is a history of chronic constipation and environmental exposures to unclean water. The patient lived in a village and owned a dog and cheeps, which he kept in the house. In addition, he has a family history of lymphoma in his brother.
On physical examination, the patient looked ill with no pallor or jaundice. There was a nonmobile, non-tender, palpable right iliac fossa mass on abdominal examination.
The laboratory data were as follows: total white blood cell count: 12 x103/mL, hemoglobin:14.4 g/dl, blood urea nitrogen: 35 mg/dl, creatinine: 0.9 mg/dl, serum albumin: 4.2 g/dL, serum bilirubin: 1 mg/dL, and negative for viral hepatitis. The urinalysis and stool examination were normal.
Ultrasonography (US) of the abdomen showed a segmental wall thickening of the ascending colon and 10x3 cm intraluminal sigmoid mass suggestive of an intestinal tumor or lymphoma. The computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest and abdomen showed that the sigmoid is redundant and seen on the right lower abdominal quadrant before its cross midline and joins the descending colon, diffuse circumferential wall thickening of the sigmoid colon, and 10x3 cm intraluminal mass with significant lumen narrowing. There were multiple perilesional lymph nodes; the largest one was measuring 1.4x1cm. There was hepatomegaly with heterogenous contrast enhancement without a definite lesion. In addition, there were multiple para-hepatic, and pulmonary lymph nodes enlargements (Figure 1). Based on the CT findings (extranodal lymph nodes enlargements and multiple general lymphadenopathies) and the family history of malignancy, the possibility of malignancy could not be excluded. After a multidisciplinary discussion, the decision was made for an open surgical exploration.
After general anesthesia and lower midline incision, the abdominal cavity was opened, revealing a sigmoid colon attached to the abdominal wall at the right lower quadrant, a large sigmoid mass measuring about 15 cm, and multiple mesenteric and paraaortic lymph nodes enlargements (Figure 2). Sigmoidectomy with a safety margins and primary anastomosis were performed, and the specimen was sent for pathologic assessment.
The postoperative period was uneventful, and he was tolerating a regular diet. The patient was discharged home on the fifth postoperative day. The histopathology reported that numerous non-caseating granulomas formed of bilharzial ova (Schistosoma mansoni) and multinucleated giant cells (Figure 3). The patient was referred to the pediatric infectious disease clinic and was treated with three doses of praziquantel (60 mg/kg). Within five months of follow-up, the patient remained symptom-free.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old boy presented in October 2021 with a 10-month history of frequent postprandial colicky generalized abdominal pain and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 10 months prior to presentation, the child experienced frequent generalized colicky abdominal pain exacerbated by eating and associated with postprandial vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, and chronic constipation.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chronic constipation. Resided in a rural village with exposure to unclean water and kept a dog and sheep inside the house. Family history was notable for lymphoma in his brother.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for anorexia, weight loss, and chronic constipation; denied hematuria, rectal bleeding, or diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-appearing without pallor or jaundice; abdominal examination revealed a non-mobile, non-tender palpable mass in the right iliac fossa.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests showed WBC 12 x 10^3/mL, hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL, BUN 35 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, total bilirubin 1 mg/dL, negative viral hepatitis serologies, and normal urinalysis and routine stool examination. Abdominal ultrasound showed segmental ascending colon wall thickening and a 10 x 3 cm intraluminal sigmoid mass.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest and abdominal CT revealed a redundant sigmoid colon extending into the right lower quadrant with diffuse circumferential wall thickening, a 10 x 3 cm intraluminal mass causing marked luminal narrowing, multiple perilesional lymph nodes (up to 1.4 x 1.0 cm), hepatomegaly with heterogeneous enhancement, and multiple enlarged para-hepatic and pulmonary lymph nodes. Exploratory laparotomy via a lower midline incision identified a 15 cm sigmoid mass adherent to the right lower quadrant abdominal wall with mesenteric and para-aortic lymphadenopathy, treated with sigmoidectomy and primary anastomosis. Histopathology of the resected sigmoid colon demonstrated numerous non-caseating granulomas containing Schistosoma mansoni ova and multinucleated giant cells without malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed colonic bilharzioma (inflammatory pseudotumor of the sigmoid colon) caused by Schistosoma mansoni on surgical histopathology, ruling out intestinal lymphoma or carcinoma. Following sigmoidectomy with primary anastomosis (discharged on postoperative day 5) and three oral doses of praziquantel 60 mg/kg, the patient remained completely asymptomatic at 5-month follow-up.
